summary.text: A cold front is the leading edge of a cooler mass of air at ground level that replaces warmer air and lies in a trough of low pressure.
The colder, drier air forms a steep boundary under the warmer, moister air and lifts it, often building tall clouds and lines of showers or thunderstorms.
Cold fronts move faster than warm fronts, can bring temperature changes as large as 30 °C (54 °F), and are stronger in fall and spring than in summer.

facts.label: Map symbol
facts.value: Blue line of triangles pointing the way it moves

facts.label: Observation code
facts.value: FROPA, logged when the front passes

items.prompt: On a weather map you spot a blue line studded with triangles. What do the triangles tell you?

options.label: Where the heaviest rain is falling
Where the coldest air is sitting
Which way the front is travelling

items.explain: A cold front is drawn as a blue line of triangles that point in the direction the front is moving.

items.prompt: When a cold front arrives, the warmer air ahead of it gets swept out of the way quickly. Why?

options.label: Cold air is denser, so it rapidly replaces the warm air
Warm air is heavier, so it sinks and drains away
Cold air carries more moisture, so it pushes harder
Sunshine heats the warm air until it vanishes

items.explain: Because cold air is denser than warm air, it quickly replaces the warm air ahead of the boundary.

items.prompt: How big can the temperature difference be from one side of a cold front to the other?
items.explain: Temperature differences across the boundary can exceed 30 °C (54 °F).

items.prompt: A cold front has just passed your town and high pressure is building behind it. What does the sky usually do next?

options.label: Fills with fog for several days

items.explain: After a cold front passes, the sky usually clears as high pressure builds in behind it.

items.prompt: A cold front reaches you after crossing a mountain range that wrung out its moisture. What is likely to happen?
items.explain: When there is not enough moisture, such as after crossing a mountain barrier, a cold front can pass without clouds.

items.prompt: You are standing outside at the moment a cold front comes through. What quick sign usually tells you it is passing?

options.label: A brief, strong gust of wind

items.explain: A quick but strong gust of wind usually shows that a cold front is passing.

paragraphs.heading: What a cold front is
paragraphs.text: A cold front is the forward edge of a cooler body of air at ground level that pushes out warmer air. It forms whenever comparatively colder air moves into a place where warmer air sits, and that leading cool air is where its name comes from. It sits in a sharp trough of low pressure near the ground.

paragraphs.heading: How it works
paragraphs.text: Cold air is denser than warm air, so it quickly takes the place of the warm air in front of the boundary. The colder, drier air wedges in under the warmer, moister air along a steep slope and lifts it. That lifting often builds tall clouds, and when there is enough moisture it can show up as a line of showers and thunderstorms. Cold fronts travel faster than warm fronts and can bring sharper changes in the weather.

paragraphs.heading: The weather it brings
paragraphs.text: Along its leading edge, a cold front usually carries a narrow band of precipitation. These bands are often intense and can bring severe thunderstorms, hail, snow squalls or tornadoes. If the air is very unstable, storms can line up in a narrow row along the front; if instability is weak, a broad sheet of rain can follow behind it instead. Anvil cirrus clouds from the storms can spread a long way downwind.

paragraphs.heading: As it passes
paragraphs.text: When a cold front arrives there is usually a quick but strong gust of wind, and weather observers log the moment with the code FROPA. Behind the front the air is cooler than the air it replaced, and the warm air is forced up, where it cools. The sky usually clears as high pressure builds in, though long bands of cumulus called cloud streets can linger if the air behind stays humid. The effects can last anywhere from hours to days.

paragraphs.heading: Seasons and strength
paragraphs.text: Cold fronts are stronger in spring and fall and weakest in summer, though their temperature changes can also be strong in the middle of winter. The temperature can differ by as much as 30 °C (54 °F) from one side of the boundary to the other. In winter a cold front can bring a cold spell and sometimes snow, yet at other times it passes with little or no precipitation. If the air is short of moisture, for instance after crossing a mountain range, a front can go by without any clouds at all.

paragraphs.heading: On the map and in the air
paragraphs.text: On weather maps a cold front is drawn as a blue line studded with triangles that point the way it is moving. Frontogenesis is the process that creates a front's temperature contrast or makes it steeper. While it happens, air circulates around the front, rising along the cold front and sinking behind it. This upward motion is what actually produces the clouds and precipitation.
